utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today we are the 12th of December 2007. I'd like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, as well as the accused and all the people present in the courtroom assisting us. We have a witness that is due to testify this afternoon. From what I understand, there are no protective measures. Is that right, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. After the witness arrived in The Hague and after further discussions, he's indicated that no protective measures are necessary, and I'll say while I'm on my feet that Mr. Flynn will be taking the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'd like to greet Mr. Flynn whom I haven't seen for a very long time. I'm happy to see him back in court today. So please bring the witness in. But in the meantime, I will give the floor to the registrar so that he can give us some exhibit numbers, please. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution has submitted its response to exhibits tendered by 1D, 3D, and 6D for Witness BB. This list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit numbers IC 747, 748, and 749 respectively. 6D has already submitted his reply to the Prosecution's response to exhibits tendered by Pusic Defence for Witness BB. This reply shall be given Exhibit number IC 750. Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Ribicic Ciril. The list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 751, the list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 752, and the list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 753. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation] [Interpretation] I have -- I was saying that a number of decisions will be recorded today, and I invite the parties to read these. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me check that you can hear properly and that you can hear the translation of what I am saying in your own language. If that is the case, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I shall ask you to kindly stand up and take the solemn declaration. Prior to that, can you give me your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Husnija Mahmutovic, born on the 3rd of March 1957 in Vares.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation, if you have one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am an official in the Vares municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you already testified before a court, whether it be before there particular court or a domestic court, on those events that unfolded in your country; and if that is the case, in which case did you testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In 1998, I think. That was in the Josip Bozic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Kindly take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You can sit down. So I'd like to provide you with a few explanations. You will be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: take much time; and, after that, the Defence counsel who are sitting to your left will put questions to you as part of the cross-examination. The Bench before you may put questions to you also, if the need arises. We shall have a break in an hour and a half approximately. If at any point in time you do not feel well, please do not hesitate to let me know so that I can stop the hearing. I shall now give the floor to the Prosecution as part of the 92 ter procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Good afternoon to Your Honours, to everybody else around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: To follow normal procedure with the 92 ter procedures which we have been adopting throughout, I will start with a brief summary, Your Honours, if that's in order. In this case, the witness was the president of the community in Stupni Do in 1993. The Croatian Defence Council took control of Vares in July 1992. They took over all the political and military functions in the municipality. The witness stated that the situation in Stupni Do and the takeover of Vares by the Croatian Defence Council. He states that after the arrival of the refugees from Kakanj, the situation for the villagers in Stupni Do became more difficult. They were often harassed when they tried to go into town. He testified -- he testifies on the ultimatum given by the Croatian Defence Council to the villagers of Stupni Do. People in Stupni Do were evacuated about 20 days in fear of an attack following that ultimatum. However, the Croatian Defence Council did not attack on that occasion. In July, the Croatian Defence Council military and political authority told the villagers that the trenches had to be filled and the villagers had to stay in Stupni Do. Afterwards, the situation for the villagers became even more difficult. Several days before the attack on Stupni Do, six Armija, Bosnian army, soldiers were arrested at the Croatian Defence Council check-points in Patafan [phoen]. Small correction here. On the 22nd of October 1993 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down somewhat, Mr. Flynn, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: On the 22nd of October 1993, the brother of a Croat woman came to take her and her husband away. On the 23rd of October 1993,, around 8.00, the Croatian Defence Council launched an attack against the village. Witness told his family to go to a shelter, and he went to a trench. The Croatian Defence Council used anti-aircraft guns. They also used inflammable ammunition. The bullet would immediately burst into flames and started to burn the houses. About an hour later, he went to his house and told the villagers to try to escape because one line of defence had been broken. He went back to the forest and stayed there until late afternoon, early evening. I put a small insertion in here. He returned to Stupni Do on the 23rd of October 1993, and he saw that his house had been burnt and property destroyed. He then went to join the others and left the village during the night. The witness indicated on a map the name of the owner of each houses and the farm in the village, and he gave -- he also gave a list of the villagers and their stature. That's a brief summary of the testimony which he gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Witness, the president asked you whether you had given testimony before any other court, either in your own country or here. Do you remember, did you testify before the Trial Chamber in the case of Kordic in 1999 in this -- in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And at the time you gave that testimony, did you answer the questions posed to you by the parties truthfully and correctly?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: When you gave your evidence during the Kordic case, you were asked a number of questions by the Prosecution and by the other parties, and you gave answers?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were those answers truthful and correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you give the answers freely, without any force or coercion?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you remember that when you travelled here to The Hague, a few days ago, you met with myself and an investigator?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And at that time, were you given an opportunity to discuss the testimony which you had given during the Kordic case?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And having gone through your testimony, does that testimony -- does the transcript accurately reflect what you told to the Trial Chamber during the Kordic case?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do the contents of the transcript reflect what you would tell the Trial Chamber here today had you to give all that evidence over again?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And I think yesterday, during our meeting, you expanded a little on that testimony, and we'll come to that shortly; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, you know that as part of the 92 bis procedure, we've already tendered the transcript in the Kordic case which is Exhibit P10015. Now, I've prepared a booklet of documents referred to in the 92 bis annex. Not all of the documents will be shown to the witness as a result of your 92 bis decision but some of them will, and I propose to deal with that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to ask you briefly at this point some general questions and to show you some documents; and if time allows, we'll come back to the actual events happening in Stupni Do on the 23rd of October. But if you remember, during your testimony to the Kordic trial panel, you stated that, in your village, you had approximately 36 to 37 soldiers in the defence unit poorly armed with little ammunition, and that was on page 10895; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you went on to say that the attack on Stupni Do started with small arms and artillery fire on the 23rd of October, on page 10906; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And between pages 10904 and 10909, you give an account of what happened: The fighting, what you saw, and what you heard. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: On then you told the Trial Chamber that on returning on the evening of the 23rd of October, you found your -- to Stupni Do, that you found your house burnt and properties destroyed, and that's on page 10908 of the Kordic transcript; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, as a result of the attack on Stupni Do on the 23rd of October 1993, were there any deaths caused as a result of this attack?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many people were killed?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Thirty-eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And when did you actually get back into your village after that first day on the 23rd of October 1993? When did you come back to Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I went back there in the early evening hours; in fact, it was in the late afternoon. It was raining, it was foggy, it was getting dark. Yes, it was getting dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you stay very long?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed there for two hours, maybe two and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And when was the next time that you returned to the village?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I went back after Vares was liberated, the second or the third day after the liberation. That might have been the 4th or the 5th of November of the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us when the bodies of the people, the 38 people, were found in the village, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: The first group of people that were found by the Nor-Bat group soldiers were put in APCs and were taken to the town cemetery in Visoko to be autopsied. The next group, so the rest of the 38 bodies in addition to the first 16, were found in the burnt-down houses. They had to be dug out, and they were identified by their next of kin.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The Panel have heard evidence that UNPROFOR, when it entered Stupni Do on the 27th of October, found 16 bodies. Can you explain to the Panel why the other bodies, the other 22 bodies, would not have been recovered or would not have been visible, if you can?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The HVO soldiers wanted to cover up the crime, and they threw the dead bodies on to the burning houses -- into the burning houses. So the houses collapsed once they burnt down, and they -- the debris covered the bodies. They deliberately burned those people in order to cover up the crime. This is what happened in my father's house. So in my father's house, I found four bodies --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were you personally involved --

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: -- charred bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were you personally involved in digging those bodies out?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were you involved in digging any other bodies, apart from those four, out?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. UNPROFOR soldiers assisted me, too, and so did the locals, the relatives of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And over what period of time did this discovery of bodies and the digging out of bodies that had not been found initially by UNPROFOR, how long did this last?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: About a month after the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And are we to assume, therefore, that a month after the attack, all 38 bodies had been recovered?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: A total of 37 bodies were found. An elderly woman was never found. We never managed to find her. And, later on, based on the statement of Radomir Rosevic, a neighbour of hers who was in America at the time, on his return, he explained that the 38th victim had been killed and thrown on to a hay stack that was then burnt down. So, in fact, they first set fire to the hay stack, and then threw the woman's body on to the hay stack, and that's why we were not able to find the 38th victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, sometime after the events in Stupni Do, was there a commission formed in the municipality to investigate the number of people who were killed and the damages caused to the properties, by the local authorities?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you take part in that process?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you prepare and present documents and lists for that commission?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were you a commissioner or sitting on the commission or were you an official working with it or were you a separate layman outside the commission?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of that commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us how did the commission operate? How did it gather -- how did it gather its information and data?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Most of the information we got from the relatives of those who had been killed were from the survivors of the attack. In most of the cases, they were able to pinpoint the exact location where a body might be found, body of their mothers, fathers, children, whoever, so that we were able to locate the bodies with a fair degree of certainty. The biggest problem we faced was when we tried to dig out the bodies because the houses were collapsing. In some cases, the victims were elderly, infirm people, who could not move, so they had -- the ceilings would just cave in and collapse on top of them. It would take us two or three days to dig, to get to those bodies, to the site where they were when they were killed, and when they were set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So did the commission or members of the commission go to the field and inspect the site of the crime, the location of where bodies were purported to have been found, and interview the family members?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, mostly the relatives were present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'd like -- you'll see a booklet in front of you of documents, and there are a number of tabs in it, like the booklet which you had yesterday. Would you turn to the -- the third tab in the booklet. It reads, "8461."

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: For the record, it's P08461.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The first part will be in English and if you proceed on you'll find the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is this a list of those killed in Stupni Do on the attack on 23rd of October 1993?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Was this prepared and signed by you?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Have you any doubts that this list is accurate?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Have you any reason to believe that any of the people mentioned in this list are still alive and living elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: In fact, I think there are a number of people with the name Mahmutovic mentioned on the list, if you go down to 16 and 17. Are these relatives of yours?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The person listed under number 16 is my brother, and the person listed under number 17 is my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity of viewing any of the bodies of the people mentioned in this list?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: How many of the people on the list did you see?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I saw all of them, with the exception of Likic, Hafit [phoen], the 38th victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Based on your observations and what were you told by family members, were you left in no doubt but that the body you viewed was the body of the name attached to that person?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, there was no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could you turn now to the next exhibit, 8462, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if you go to the last page of the Bosnian version you'll find a signature at the bottom of the page. Please tell us if you recognise that signature.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is this list another list that you prepared of destroyed and burned houses that were burned in the attack on Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And I think when we went through it yesterday, there was a total of approximately 76 individuals who had their property damaged; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And, again, for the purposes of preparing this list, did you take information from the occupants or owners of the properties to attribute -- that would lead to you attribute it to the attack on Stupni Do on the 23rd-24th of October?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: The village was not big. I knew all the villagers, all the locals. I was in every house, and I knew well how people lived there and what possessions they had, what movables and immovables they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Have you any doubt that any of the property mentioned in this list that you're looking at now was not caused as a result of the attack on Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Looking at the list that you prepared, have you any doubt --

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: -- that the property was not damaged as a result of the attack on Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: All the property in the list was destroyed or burned down completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if you go then to the next list, it's 8463.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: For the record, P08463.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Tell me when you have it.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The title of this is, "A list of devastated cattle found during the attack on Stupni Do." Is this another list and document that you prepared for the benefit of the commission, signed by you on the second page?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is my signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And, again, are you satisfied that the contents of this list are truthful and accurate and that all of the damage or all the loss of property referred to on the list can be attributed to the attack on Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, I want you to look at one more exhibit for me, please, if you go to Exhibit 8377. When you have it, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Panel what this is, please?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: A special commission was appointed on behalf of Vares municipality, with Muhamed Sabanovic, architect and engineer; Omer Kadric, engineer and economist; and Hajrudin Vezir, a construction engineer. They toured all the torched houses in the local commune of Stupni Do. They measured the area, they took photos of all the houses, and compiled a record based on what they had seen in the field. Every property owner, every house owner, if they were alive, was present, together with them, so they could measure everything and they could make the record of the damage that had been inflicted upon every household. This is just one of the series of those records, and this record reflects the damage to my family house.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if we go to the last part in the record, we have a photograph. Is this a -- does this photograph depict your family home following the attack on Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was a completely new house, and a completely equipped house.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, on the subject of the houses, can you tell us if any of the houses in the village including your house had anywhere to shelter in the events of an attack? Had they any special part set aside?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Under the law that prevailed in former Yugoslavia, if you were to be given a building permit, your design had to incorporate a shelter, a shelter in case there was a war or a chemical attack. So every newer house, i.e., recently constructed house, a house that was built after 1980-something, I don't know the exact year, but I know that every new development had to have a concrete shelter that had to be adjacent to the cellar of the new-built; otherwise, the commission that had to approve your house for habitation would not approve it if it did not have the so-called atomic shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And would it be correct to say that she is shelters were stronger than the other part of the house?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were made of reinforced concrete, and they mostly did not have any windows. They only had a door and some ventilation shafts.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did any of these houses -- did any of these rooms or basements have outside protection?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My house, for example, had very thick wooden panels on the outer windows that protected it from shelling. The house that you're looking at, it had windows at the bottom part and they were sheltered with sandbags; and, behind those, there were wooden panels, very thick wooden beams, in case of attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us, could any of the rooms or basements within the village, which were used for these protective -- as these protective shelters, could they have been used or converted into a fortified command post or a bunker from which one could conduct a determined defence?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you told us -- you told the Trial Panel in the Kordic case that you came down to your family, and you told your family to leave for the forest. Where had your family been at that time?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: My family was in the atomic shelter in this very house. What you see beneath in white brick, that was the basement, and the shelter was under the ground and it was made of reinforced concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And apart from your family - and I don't need to you mention any names just yet - but apart from your family, was anybody else in this basement, sheltering with your family?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: There were neighbours. In this particular street, there were five more families. So all those families were there, save for the handicapped persons who stayed at home. There were two such people. So apart from those two people, everybody else was together with my family, a total of 17 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, so you had this protective room where they were hiding. Despite the fact that they were hiding there, were your family safe or did something happen to them during the attack on Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: My family was safe from shelling and from any external influences. However, when the HVO troops arrived, they started going from one house to the next, from one basement to the next, and chased people out of those premises. They killed people in front of their houses. They burned them alive. They had lined them up first. Out of the 17 that I mentioned, four were killed; three fled on my order to the forest beneath the houses, a small thicket; the rest were lined up, plundered, raped. Behind this house was my brother's house. The rest -- the remainder of them were locked in that house, and they torched the house. These people burned alive. Luckily enough, they still remained alive. They didn't die; and how this came about, only they can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us that in the shelter on that occasion, do you know if there was somebody by the name of Rasida Likic, in your shelter?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did she survive the attack?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to her?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: She was killed because she had told them, "Don't touch us," and I quote her: "You can take anything from the house, just leave us alone," then one of the soldiers fired a bullet into her, and that's how she died.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And was this something you witnessed or something that you came to learn about later?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there. I learned that subsequently from the survivors.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us, does the name Mehmed Likic mean anything to you? Was this person also in the shelter on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those people were actually disabled.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did Mehmed Likic survive the attack?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No. He was killed also.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Does the name Rifet Likic mean anything to you? Was he in the basement?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Rifet Likic was a neighbour of mine. He was a very nice young man, and he was disabled. His both feet were deformed. That's how he was born. It was congenital, and he was not fit for the military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: We don't have much time now. I just need to know if he was in the basement --

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: His throat was slit. He was in the basement, and his throat was slit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, you have to finish now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm almost finished, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The last question: Your father, Zejnil Mahmutovic, was he killed during the attack?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was killed, above the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few follow-up questions. You were in the village at the time of the attack. Did you have a weapon at the time?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had a hunting carbine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you fire a shot?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, around the village, were there any shelters or bunkers to protect the village, around the village, I mean?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, near the village. And those were used by the civilian population in case of shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Bogos hill which is just next door, were there any soldiers on that hill top.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And they were defending the hill, were they?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a strategic elevation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Out of 224 inhabitants, there were 36 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These 36 soldiers, were they part of the so-called Territorial Defence or were they part of an ABiH unit or affiliated to such a unit?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: At first, at the beginning of the conflict or the war, they were Territorial Defence. That's what they were called. Later on, they joined or they became the BiH army, so one can say that they were BiH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among these 36 soldiers, was anyone in charge? Was there a commander, somebody who was in command of these 36 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No. The true commander of that unit had been arrested seven days prior to that at the check-point in Mala Rijeka. The HVO had the check-point there; and on my insisting, they headed for home. They were in Breza in a small town near Vares. They headed home because I had sent a message that something was happening in Vares, and there was something wrong there, and they were arrested, the six of them. I went to the head of the HVO municipality to let them go, but he wouldn't do that. So during the attack on Stupni Do, they were in the HVO prison in Vares, and I suppose that under the torture, they said what they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me get back to the village. The commander had been arrested a week before. Weren't you acting as a commander? Yes, da. So you were the commander of those soldiers who were there. You were acting commander, weren't you? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I was not a commander, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So was nobody there in charge? Who in military terms was in charge then?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: There were squad leaders. One of them was Suad Likic. Those were people who did not have much knowledge about the doctrine of warfare or the doctrine of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... that you went off into the forest; and if I've understood you well, the HVO had not completely surrounded the village because you were able to escape. If you were able to escape, there must have been escape holes.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: There was an exit. We didn't know exactly where they were because fire was opened from all sides; and at that moment, we didn't know how to escape, how to leave the village. The village is located in a valley, It's surrounded by the hill tops, and fire was being opened from all those hill tops, from all sorts of weapons. It was only in the evening that some of the survivors managed to escape to a rocky part of the thicket, following the little path that goes behind this house that is depicted in this photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you went into that direction also, did you?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No. I went in an opposite direction. I passed by the HVO soldiers at some 100 metres distance, by the check-points that they put up during the night after the end of the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my last question now. You have told us that shots were fired. You told us that you were made aware of the fact that there were HVO soldiers. How many were there, 20, 50, 100, or do you have no idea?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: There was a huge number of them. The terrain is of that aspect that if you were to line them up next to each other, there were a lot of them; but, later on, I learned that about 500 men participated in that attack. So, in addition to the men who had been brought from Kiseljak, from the so-called Maturice and Apostoli, there were also people from the villages that are located around Stupni Do, which were predominantly inhabited by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have two brief questions to put to you. In the transcript on page 17, line 11, 12, and 13, today's transcript, you have said that your family was saved and were not hit by the shells. You also said that some people were burned alive. What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: You did not understand me properly, Your Honour. Those people who were not executed in front of the house that you see on the screen, some of them were looted. They even tried to slaughter my younger son. At one point, when Rifet's throat was slit, this same man approached the five or six year old boy and tried to slit his throat. My wife was in his house robe, and he had a very thick gold chain around the neck. When he approached the young child, he saw the chain, he grabbed the chain, snatched it from my wife, and he forgot all about the child. But the child was so scared that, from that moment on, he could not speak for some six months; and even when he spoke -- started speaking, he started stuttering. The remainder of the persons, save for those four that had been killed, were taken to a house behind the house that you see in the photo. They locked them in, they were alive, and they set the house on fire. That was just before they started pulling out of the village. The house started burning, and they continued walking. The centre of the village is below my house. Then when this house started burning and when these people started suffocating in the house, they used an ax. They broke out of the houses, and that's how they survived. They fled to the forest. So they did not burn alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. I did say I had two questions. You partly answered my second question because you said that there was somebody who was a child under age, and the other people that were shut up in the house and that burnt. Were all these people civilians?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sir, a while ago, you told us that your house was, so to speak, fortified; in other words, there were sandbags in front of the windows. You added that nobody had fired a shot from that house and could not be used as a fortress, so to speak. In the village, were there other houses, one or several others, that were reinforced in the same way and that could have been used as a defence fortification, where somebody might have fired shots from against the attackers.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No. There were a few houses; for example, the command building was fortified and this house is in the meadow below my house. It was fortified, but at the moment there was nobody there. As for the rest of the houses, people were scared, and they spontaneously withdrew to the other part of the village; and at one point, only one of the villagers, my cousin and my deputy in the civilian sector, who was also a member of the committee that looked after the village, when they approached close enough to kill the other civilian, he threw two grenades from the immediate vicinity. According to him, he had wounded some of them, and that's how they had given up on any further attacks. So there was no fire opened from any of the houses. People just grouped and tried finding shelter where they thought that they would be safer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question and then I will give the floor to the Defence. So we had a witness who told us that somebody had come from Vares a few days before to ask the villagers to hand in their weapons, and that the villages did not want to hand in their weapons; is this true or not? What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: That was not seven days before that. It was around the 20th or the 21st of June of that same year. I don't know whether it was just their tactic or something that existed in all of their orders. They simply called me and asked me to inform the military commander that all the weapons in the village had to be handed over; and in return they would feed us, they would give us humanitarian aid, and that they would defend us from the Serbian side. I returned to the village, I called a meeting. I informed the commander, but we knew from experience what the surrender of weapons meant and that it would only mean death for us. We did not want to hand the weapons over. That was two months before. They gave us an ultimatum, and they told us that they would attack us if we did not hand our weapons over by 7.00 that morning. At the meeting, we decided not to surrender the weapons. The village nearby called Dastansko did surrender their weapons, and they were treated very badly. We knew from experience what it meant to hand over one's weapons, and that's why we didn't -- that's why we didn't hand them over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those who handed their weapons in the village next door, you said that they were badly treated or suffered a very --

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Because when they handed over the weapons, the other side didn't really trust, didn't believe that all the weapons had been handed over, and that is quite natural. So the villagers had to leave, go to the neighbouring villages. All the men of military age had to do that. They had to go to the neighbouring villages to the BH army-controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us that you had a hunting rifle and that you were very badly equipped. What could you do against people who were better armed, who were greater in number? Wasn't it dangerous to just keep a few weapons, as you did?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we had the superior command, too, in the village of Dabravina, and we notified them that night. The weapons that were obtained with such great difficulties, we didn't want to and we couldn't surrender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the Supreme Command had told you, "Keep your weapons," is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So who will begin? Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Witness, everybody in the courtroom, good afternoon to all of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, My name is Vesna Alaburic. I'm an attorney from Zagreb, and I'm representing General Petkovic at this trial. I will be asking you some questions primarily regarding the defence of Stupni Do, and some questions generally related to the defence in accordance with the regulations and rules of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As a follow-up to Judge Antonetti's question whether the military unit in Stupni Do was part of the Territorial Defence or the BH army, and you said -- you gave your reply, but I would just like you to explain to the Judges what happened with the terms, the names that were used. So I would like to ask you to look at document 4D 404, 404, in the set of documents that you have. You will see there are stickers at the side. That's 404.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you've seen this document, but I'm sure that you will be familiar with the contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document has already been admitted as an exhibit. This is an order of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina signed by Alija Izetbegovic dated the 23rd of June 1992, where it says that the name, the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, shall be changed to the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, could you please tell us, this is precisely what you told His Honour Judge Antonetti, that the Territorial Defence became the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So from June 1992 onwards, we can say, we can only speak about the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in accordance with this decision of the BH Presidency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Could we now look at the defence of the village of Stupni Do. Mr. Mahmutovic, could you please tell us who was the commander of the BH army unit in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Esel [phoen] Likic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You told us that he was one of the six members of the army that were arrested on the 18th of October 1993; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name of Ekrem Mahmutovic?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please make pauses between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was the commander of the tactical group according to my information; but at the time of the attack, he was not there. He was no where near the area in fact. He was not anywhere near Stupni Do or Vares.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So can we then say that he was the commander of a military units of the BH army? We don't want to go into all the details whether it's a tactical group.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to draw your attention, Your Honours, that under 4D 869, I've prepared for you a statement by Mr. Ekrem Mahmutovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, let me now put to you some of the things that he said, and now we will try to determine what is actually true and what is not. Mr. Ekrem Mahmutovic, in his statement, said that after the arrest of Mr. Likic, who was the commander of the unit of the BH army in Stupni Do, that actually you took over his post as the president of the local commune. Regardless of the fact that you answered a similar question asked to you by Judge Antonetti, can you please tell us whether this statement made by Mr. Ekrem Mahmutovic is correct or not?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that after Mr. Likic's arrest in Stupni Do, there was no commander of all those squads in this BH army platoon, so there was no one commander?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I explained to His Honour that there were just the squad leaders. I know one of them. I know -- and I gave the name to the Trial Chamber. Suad Likic was the commander of one of the squads.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you're trying to tell us that there was no single commander in Stupni Do who would be in command of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, please. Please make a break between questions and answers because you're speaking the same language and we have a problem then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, we understand what you told us about the squads. My question now is whether what you answered meant that there was no single person who would be in charge or superior to all of the commanders of those squads.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I know that this one person was the commander or leader of one squad. Now, whether he commanded all of them during the attack, I don't know that. We didn't have any radio stations, we didn't have any Motorolas. But at the time of the attack, there was a large circle around the village. So a lot of the front line was not covered, and there was virtually or absolutely no coordination among the soldiers. We had some trenches that were four or five kilometres away from each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Fine. We will go back to the trenches, to the radio stations and the radio sets and the communication that you were table to maintain. But now I would like to address the issue of weapons. You mentioned that you had a hunting rifle. Could you please tell me other members of the BH army, what kind of weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: As for the exact number of weapons, I don't know that. But that would be up to maybe 30 rifles: Old rifles, newer rifles, PAP rifles, semi-automatic rifles, and there were maybe five or six. The PAP rifles are semi-automatic rifles, there were maybe five or six automatic rifles,, and there was a mortar that was never used. It was not used on that day either.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So this would be the 60-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the rockets launcher, what would that be?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about any rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You never heard of it?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And did you hear about anyone being in possession of hand grenades or bombs in the village?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: People did have hand grenades. They would buy them. They actually, the two hand grenades that one of the household heads had, actually saved many lives because the massacre would have been even worse.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell us how many bullets did you have?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I personally had 80 bullets for this rifle, the hunting carbine rifle. Now, as to how many bullets there were in the village, how many bullets the BH army soldiers had, I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how long did the effort of the HVO to take the village of Stupni Do last? How long did the fighting last, half an hour, an hour?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: From 8.00 -- ten minutes past 8.00 in the morning until the afternoon, maybe two or three in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So that would mean that the fighting took maybe five or six hours?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I didn't have a watch on me, but I know that it did last some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Please tell us, although you don't remember and you don't know how many HVO troops were involved, but could you please tell us whether the HVO soldiers were well armed?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us how come that it took the well-armed and probably numerous HVO forces six hours to take the village of Stupni Do? Was the resistance offered by the BH army so fierce that the fighting had to last six hours?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: The lads that were deployed above the village in the Lipa sector, as it was called, offered the fiercest resistance. They resisted for the whole of that day. Actually, that trench was never taken. As for the rest, the village is surrounded by the woods. It took four hours of fighting before they actually managed to leave the wooded area and get to the meadows, because the village is where you first have the houses, then you have two or three kilometres of meadows, and then the wooded area. And, of course, the HVO soldiers didn't really feel like going out in the open. I think that was the reason why they didn't take the village all that quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, could you please tell me, do you know how many HVO soldiers were killed or wounded in this attack?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But do you know that the HVO suffered casualties?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us how you know that?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was told later that ambulances came in after Abid Likic -- after the wounding by the hand grenade, and then they picked up those casualties, dead or wounded, and took them to Vares.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In one of the reports on the people who were killed, you said that there were 220 inhabitants in the village and eight displaced persons at the time of the attack. Is that an accurate piece of information?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this number may have varied by two or one, two or three, because people left through -- left the village. They went out through the woods in order to get some food, because we were no longer allowed to go to Vares and to buy food there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, regarding the knowledge of the HVO plan for the attack on Stupni Do, I will now read a part of the statement by Ekrem Mahmutovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Croatian -- or rather, B/C/S, that would be on page 11 and 12; and in the English version, that is on page 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So Ekrem Mahmutovic says the following, I quote: "On the 21st of October 1993, when the HVO unit arrived in Vares, the War Presidency in exile ordered the evacuation of the village of Stupni Do because there was a rumour that the HVO might attack Stupni Do and Dastansko." So, Mr. Mahmutovic, have you ever heard of there decision of the War Presidency in exile on the evacuation of Stupni Do or not?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: The evacuation plan did exist. But that evening we did not receive any orders to evacuate, or anything else; except, except for something that I could only guess or speculate about when the brother of a Croat who was Croat woman who was married to a neighbour of mine by the name of Alija. When he came into the village, picked up his sister, and Alija, his brother-in-law, he took them away from Stupni Do. So it was some kind of an alarm. It rang the alarm bell that there might be an attack. I didn't know anything about the evacuation, and I didn't do anything to that end.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Mr. Ekrem Mahmutovic says in his statement that this code for the evacuation was broadcast via radio communications to Stupni Do and that the signalman in Stupni Do radioed back that the villagers refused to leave the village. But they insisted that if they come under an attack, they should get assistance.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's first focus on radio communications. Not only Ekrem Mahmutovic but many other witnesses spoke about radio communications and the signalman who was in Stupni Do. Mr. Mahmutovic, do you know anything about the fact that Stupni Do had radio communications with the -- with any BH structures, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did have radio set. It was an RUP 1, 2 or 3. I don't know what it was called. They had it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, let me finish. Nobody from the military structures notified me about anything, including this thing that there was this warning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, but were you aware that it was possible to communicate, or rather, that there was this communication via radio that night, regardless of whether you were involved in it or not?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what did you know? Were you aware of this order and the refusal to obey it?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What did you know about this exchange of messages?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I have to wait for the interpretation. I knew that there was a radio set. All the local communes had such sets. All the local communes in the Vares municipality had radio sets or radio stations. They were used for civilian or military purposes alike. If somebody got sick, it would be used. While the HVO was in Vares, we communicated with them. If anyone got sick, then that person could be taken down.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the technical possibility to communicate. I'm asking you about the contents of the radio messages that were exchanged on the 22nd of October 1993, on the eve of the attack. Were you aware that anyone was sending any messages to anyone that some warnings were sent out and that somebody in the village decided to -- that the population should remain?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please not overlap?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer was no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you another statements by the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is page 10 in the English text.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Ekrem Mahmutovic says, and I quote: "I was in Breza. Around 1900 hours on the 22nd October 1993, when we received a message from Stupni Do sent by radio that something might happen in Stupni Do. Husnija Mahmutovic ordered his signalsman to send a coded message to Breza, and the message was that Alija Likic had informed him that Stupni Do would be attacked by the HVO." Mr. Mahmutovic, can you confirm whether this is the truth or not?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Whatever Ekrem Mahmutovic stated, he learned only subsequently, much, much later. And whatever he stated here, I believe is a blatant lie because after this crime, people exaggerated, distorted things. And since he was personally an inhabitant of that local commune, as a commander, he should have known more.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, I don't know what the relationship between the two of you is. I only want to hear the truth, and I want to hear whether there is accord or discord between you in these matters. Tell me, please, whether you have any knowledge that the villagers of the village had meetings, that they tried to decide what to do, and that they made a certain decision on the eve of the attack on the 22nd of October?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: In the evening, I informed the Crisis Staff, which consisted of elderly and rather serious people, and we decided to reinforce the guard duty, to step up the guard duty, in case of attack. However, during the night, we could not see anything different from the things that had been happening before. There were no movements of soldiers or anything that could alert us to the fact that in the sector of Stupni Do or in its vicinity, there would be an attack the following morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the Kordic case, you said that the municipality council had a meeting and decided that all the villagers of the village should be mobilised and that the village should prepare itself for defence. Is this more or less what you have just tried to tell us?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For a year and a half, we had been in prison; and for a year and a half, we had been mobilised every night.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that, Mr. Mahmutovic. I really want to you tell us everything that happened. You also said, in the Kordic case, that some days before the attack, the trenches had been dug out and that the preparations had been carried out for medical assistance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in case of attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You also said that from before, there had been some shelters and trenches, that there had been sandbags and water prepared; and on the eve of the attack, you only inspected all those locations. You repaired whatever was necessary to repair, and you had a short first aid course. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that on the 22nd of October, you undertook everything that was possible in order to prepare the village for defence?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, the trenches around the village, what was the distance between the first line of those trenches and the first houses in the village alone?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What was the distance between the trenches and the first houses in the village of Stupni Do itself?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Some were three kilometres away, some were six kilometres away, some five. It depended on the configuration of the ground. The farthest trench was on Bogos hill on the strategic trigger points which was some seven kilometres away from the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when it comes to the defence of the village, did you organise it in such a way that even the most distant trenches would be manned by the defenders who would bar the entrance to the village?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in the course of the attack, the BiH army abandoned some of those trenches that were far away from the village and that they started approaching the village itself?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: They abandoned just the one trench, the trench facing Bijelo Borje. Those were very inexperienced young men. Actually, 99 per cent had their first encounter with attack with rifles, with fire. So a few of the lads abandoned the trench and ran towards the village. Those men on Bogos, they died; and as for the third trench, that was facing the village of Mir, they could not leave the village because of the configuration of the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now I'm interested in the approach of the BiH army troops to the centre of village.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A lot of people have spoken about that in this case. I can prepare all of their statements for after the break. But in nutshell we can summarise them by saying that the defence during the attack --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, were you granted more time by other lawyers?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as I know, only Praljak Defence and Petkovic Defence have prepared cross-examination. General Praljak needs some 15 [as interpreted] minutes, and the remainder of the time belongs to me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, there have been people who -- here who have told us about the defence of the village approaching the centre of the village, and I'm going to quote some of those statements, which stated that the Defence approached houses that served as shelters. For example, Mr. Ejub Likic said that Salih Likic was killed in the area around the shelter which was defended by 14 members of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, I'm going to say that this is Exhibit number P08121, item 27 AF.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic is it correct that 14 members of the BH army were defending the shelter which housed the civilians in the very centre of the village, i.e., in the village of Stupni Do itself?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: It's not correct. It's not correct, and I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What is not correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: It is not correct --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What is not correct, the figure of 14 or that there were any members of the BiH army defending that shelter and that building?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: From the position where I was, I could not see that part of the village where the entire civilian population had withdrawn to. But I know that at the moment of the attack, and some hour or an hour and a half into attack, there was completes chaos and Ejub Likic's statement is not correct because he himself had also fled the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's analyse what you've just told us, please. You have told us that you did not see the part of the village to which the civilian population had withdrawn to. Does that mean that all of those 200-some civilians had withdrawn to that one part of the village that you yourself couldn't see?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And tell us, please, were they all in one central shelter?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And when you say that Mr. Ejub Likic is not saying the truth because he had fled, can you just tell us briefly what the problem may be, what was his problem?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Ejub Likic was on Bogos hill which was a very strategically important point at which lads had died. At the moment when the trench was falling, he left the mortar that was up there. He had not fired a single shell. He just left it there and he ran down to the village without a rifle, without a hand grenade. There were several lads who had done that, so there was a chaos everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in the village itself, where was the position of the mortar. In the village itself, where was the mortar in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: It had been taken to Bogos hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So in the village, there was no mortar?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ejub Likic also stated that Amit Likic another member of the BH army from that position, near the shelter in which there were civilians, threw a hand grenade at the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The exhibit is the same, at item 27 AI and AK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another blatant lie, and can I explain?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We don't have the time unfortunately. You've already heard Their Honours rushing me. I just wanted to show you another statement before the break. Avdija Likic stated the following: "The defence forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina were focused around the main shelter in the village, where there was a majority of the civilians." This was Ejub Likic's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The exhibit number is P06978, item 38 C.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Mahmutovic, this is another person's statement about the concentration of the Defence forces of the BiH army around the main village shelter; is it true or not true?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Not true. There could have been two or three soldiers, but 14? No. That's beyond belief.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Ejub mentioned the number of 14; Avdija speaks about a high concentration, but that doesn't matter. Before we start talking about civilian population, there is another important detail. Mr. Avdija Likic stated that the HVO had called civilian population of the Stupni Do to surrender in the course of fighting, but that the BiH army refused to surrender and decided to continue fighting despite the situation on the ground. Tell us, please, whether that is correct or not?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Lie, lie.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, I would like to say that this is the same exhibit number, item 38 D. Now, Your Honours, I find this a convenient time for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely right, but there is just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, there are two documents, 080182 [as interpreted] and 06978. These are P-documents. It's Prosecution documents, aren't they? Because in your binder, I can not find them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these are statements of the witnesses that have already been admitted into evidence. Those were not viva voce witnesses. They were witnesses whose statements we adopted in this case. Unfortunately, I've not prepared them because they were not important, and I don't want to tender them into evidence. They were just the basis for putting questions to this witness, and I have provided the references to the specific items in the statements so the statements may be checked. If you so wish, I can prepare both of these statements for the session that starts after the break, so you may be able to verify all the -- everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you not continue for ten more minutes, and that way we can take a break at 5.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: With your permission, I would like to put a question to the witness. Witness, you stated not long ago, very clearly, that it was a mistake to say that the HVO had invited the inhabitants of Stupni Do and the defenders of Stupni Do to surrender. How can say that it was not true when were you so far from the area where the civilians were? Is it not possible that there was such a call but that you simply had not heard it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From conversations, Your Honour, from conversations with the people who had thrown grenades, with the person who had defended those civilians. Drugged soldiers had killed at random so nobody stood a chance in hell to remain alive. They killed everybody. There was no chance for anybody to remain alive, or for them to call anybody to surrender. If you can appreciate the situation as it was on that day, them calling somebody to surrender is beyond belief. I spoke to people, to the civilians who were in that shelter. Nobody ever called to anybody to surrender, and I really don't know where this statement came from. How could anybody have stated this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you put the question clearly to the person you spoke to? Did you ask them whether they heard anything, a call, a speech, or somebody from the -- or something from the HVO? I understand that there was a moment when people were firing shots and nobody was careful. But if I have understood you well, people were cautioned, and this preceded the time you have just spoken about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is the first time, since 12 or 13 years ago, do I hear somebody saying that somebody called somebody. After so many stories and things told, after the end, this is the first time I hear from anybody that people had been called to surrender, which obviously shows you this is not true. Can you imagine 200 or 300 men firing at a handful of people? I really, really don't understand this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, we have had witness here. We have had women who spoke about that. One of them was a messenger, but we won't go into that. Now I would like to talk about the civilians.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, if I may interrupt you. I really can't stay calm. If the Trial Chamber would allow me, I would like to explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask to you leave that to the end of today's session, because my time is really restricted. I would like to explain for the Trial Chamber something else, and I believe that you are the ideal person to help us with that. The list of the fallen persons, my learned friends Flynn showed you that under 58641. This is the list of 38 people, and I suppose that you know very well who these people are. You're familiar with the list, but I would like to show you one person on number 28, Rasema Likic. I would like to tell you that for that person, one witness, a female witness whose name is Salifa [phoen] Likic. Said as following -- as follows: "While they were hiding in the forest, one elderly woman died. She had been identified as Rasema Likic. She probably died from exhaustion or a heart attack."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the statement under P06798, item 19 F.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, do you have any knowledge about Rasema Likic having died in the forest after she had managed to leave Stupni Do, rather than having been killed in Stupni Do itself?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That woman died at the exit. Her heart stopped from fear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, before we start talking about the civilians, let's try to clarify, for the benefit of the Judges, the words "CZ" next to some of the names. Does this abbreviation stand for "civilian protection," to help you answer?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us please, the civilian protection, was that one of the forms or aspects of the defence activities of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the same was true of the citizens of Croatia and all of the other citizens of the former Yugoslavia? Can we agree on that, that the civilian protection was one form of defence activity?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But our civilian protection looked after the civilian population, and dug out trenches around the villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please now look at 4D 00408?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a decree on defence, the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The date is November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I believe it would be very useful if we could together explain to the Trial Chamber what were the rights and duties of the citizens in defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at Article 46 of this decree.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I believe you're waiting for the document to appear on the screen, but you have it in your binder, article 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
