utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for being fastidious. But according to the transcript on line 6, page 44, you have said that the date of the decree is November 1992. I'm looking at the first page, at any rate, of the translated version we have, and we have the date of the 20th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're perfectly right, as regards the passing of the decree itself; but it was published in the Official Gazette in November 1992. So that when I said November, I actually was referring to the time of the publication. But the date that was mentioned by His Honour Judge Trechsel was, in fact, more important, because the decree enters into force on the date of its passing, not publication.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So could we please look at this Article in front of us, 46?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document here says that this is a copy of the Narodni List of the Official Gazette. But I think there is a slippage here between the original and the translation, because I see here that in the original text, we have the date 15th of November. I don't think one needs to be a linguist to understand this. This might be a translation error. Please proceed. I don't wish to delay you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are right, as usual. There is a mistranslation here on top, and I have to admit that I did not pay any attention to that particular part of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So at any rate, Article 46, let us look at the rights and obligations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: -- of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina in defence. It says here that they have military obligation. So let us take it one at a time. Citizens are under the military obligation. Was military obligation one of the obligations that the citizens had in the defence of their country?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: As far as Article 46 is concerned, in the case of Stupni Do, the civilians and the civil defence --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, we will get to that.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: The civil defence had only the right to be killed without the rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We will get to the civil defence, civilian protection; or, in fact, I just want to show the Judges what are the obligations of the citizens in the defence of the country, and that this was just a pretext for me to do so. So military obligation is number 1 obligation?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The second one is work obligation?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at Article 48, so that our judges are able to get a picture --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... you said so. The people who were part of the civil defence, according to what you know, were these people around in your village or were they not? I'm talking about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour, for a year and a half, we were under a media blockade. We could only see one TV channel, and everything that is now shown on the screen is something that I may have got my hands on after the war. But during the war, all those Official Gazettes and everything, that is now being shown to me, that is nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not asking about the media. I'm talking about your fellow citizens who were in your village and who were part of the civil defence. Were these people armed or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not armed, Your Honour. They were not armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's what I wanted to know. We need to have a break now. It is 5.00, and we are having a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I wonder if I may, before Ms. Alaburic continues, I had wanted to say this, but I didn't want to break her train of thought when she was cross-examining. Just by way of record, on page 38, at line 6, Ms. Alaburic, when she was questioning the witness, suggested that there had been a lot of people who had told us various things for the Tribunal here, concerning what had happened in the village of Stupni Do; then she proceeded to put to the witness the statements of certain people, including Ejub Likic, another Likic member whose name I can't pick up from the transcript; then she referred to various exhibits, some of which were P exhibits. Just for the record, I want to say that these are not 92 bis witnesses. Those are not witnesses who ever testified in any shape or form before the Tribunal. And as far as I can see from looking at P exhibits over the break, they are effectively statements which were collected by the UNPROFOR military police or various other law enforcement officers who were investigating Stupni Do in the course of the investigation which took place afterwards. So they are statements which were untried and untested. I just wanted that to be on the record because she had introduced them as statements from people who had told us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's been recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, my learned colleague, Mr. Flynn, is completely right. This is all about the relaying of the statements made by those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So but let us go back to the rights and duties of the citizens of BH in the defence of the country. We mentioned the military obligation, which is self-evident, and then we have the work obligation. And can we now look at Article 48 which is in front of you on the screen. Could we please try and explain to the Judges what that is? You know that as the president of the local commune. So in accordance with the ordinance on defence, all citizens able to work, above the age of 15, were under the work obligations. The work obligation could be carried out in the organs of the state administration, companies, and other legal persons, and it could also be discharged by carrying out temporary work for the needs of the defence. So you do know what the work defence is, Mr. Mahmutovic?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, in the former Yugoslavia, and in all the countries of the former Yugoslavia, was it a rule that people above the age of 15 could be put under an obligation to work in a state organ or a company that is vital for the defence? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And was there a rule that citizens, mostly men who were under the work obligation, did not have to serve in the army; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that, in fact, the work and military obligations are actually complementary; in other words, a single person can be either under the military obligation or under the work obligation? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please speak up, because your answer was not recorded in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So it is clear that the work obligation is one of the forms of the defence of the country, is that so?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In normal conditions, it is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, we will see what the situation is like in wartime conditions. The next thing that is mentioned in Article 46 is civilian protection. You gave some explanation when Judge Antonetti asked, but let us see what is stipulated in greater detail in Articles 72 of this ordinance. I will read. So this is Article 72, and it says that the civilian protection shall be organised, prepared, and carried out as a system of the protection and rescue of people, physical, and cultural property against wartime destruction, natural disasters, industrial disasters, and all the other risks in peace and wartime. Was this the task of the civilian protection, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, members of the civilian protection, through their work in the civilian protection, contributed to the defence of the country; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Members of the civilian protection were not at the same time soldiers and were not under the work obligation, is that so?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In Article 51, one of the obligations imposed on the citizens -- rather, I apologise. It is not Article 51; it is Article 47, paragraph 3. There is an interesting obligation that is imposed on the citizens, and let me quote: "They shall provide information pertinent for the defence that they learn or observe, and they shall provide them to the alerting centre or state organs as soon as possible." Mr. Mahmutovic, does that mean that the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina were under the obligation to inform those alerting centres about any information that is relevant for the defence of the country and to contribute to the defence of their country in this manner?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, who defended the Accused Kordic, in your previous testimony, showed you the statement by Mr. Ekrem Mahmutovic, who had said that there were 50 soldiers in Stupni Do; not 36 or 37, as you indicated. When this was put to you by Mr. Naumovski, you replied, and I quote: "Everybody served. There were old age pensioners and others." Did I quote you right? Did you say that everybody served in the defence of the country?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But there is this difference: Some were armed and others just had spades.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But the fact that some had spades was due to the fact that they had their own tasks in the defence of the country?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, on the 3rd of November 1998, you said that "all healthy men of military age in the village were under an obligation to join the Territorial Defence which later became the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But that was on a voluntary basis, because we didn't have the police. We didn't have any kind of system, or anything of that sort, that would force those who were unwilling or punish them so that they join the army. So everything was on a voluntary basis, precisely because the village had been under a siege or had been encircled for a year and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This was, as you indicated right at the beginning of the Territorial Defence. But Mr. Mahmutovic I would now like to focus on civilians and see how out of those maybe 200 civilians - you may correct this figure - how they managed to leave the village of Stupni Do. You have told us that they were located in the houses that served as shelters, and you told us something that is quite interesting. It is something that I, as a lawyer, with quite some experience and of -- in fact, I can't recall any law that bound the civilians building their private homes to have atomic shelters in their houses. I consulted my colleagues from other parts of the former Yugoslavia, from Sarajevo, and they also were unaware of this regulation. So I put it to that you this is not correct, what you said, that private homes in Bosnia-Herzegovina had to be equipped with shelters in case of an attack. Would you agree with me, despite what you had said earlier?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. So in those shelters, atomic shelters, as you put it, there were maybe some 200 civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us, we can use your list to ascertain how many civilians were killed, some 20 or so, could you please tell us how did the 150 to 180 people manage to leave Stupni Do and to save their lives? To begin with, can you please tell us when they left Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: They left in the night. It was -- it stopped raining, but it was overcast and foggy. The HVO troops withdrew to the hills around the village, to the check-points around the village. They set up fires, and I know that because I passed by one such check-point. The column moved out when they saw that --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic --

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Let me finish, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, no, please, because we will not be able to go through everything that I want to go through. You said, "during the night," so could you tell us where were these people during that day?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: In their shelters, or as you put it, the atomic shelters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, that was the term you used, and I quoted you when I used that term. But that's immaterial now. At the time, when the HVO soldiers entered the village, the villagers were in the shelters?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The villagers, for the most part, remained in shelters after the HVO soldiers left the village; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the HVO soldiers did not go from house to house and did not look into the shelters where civilians were at the time?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I explained a little while ago, the HVO soldiers stopped the attack after one of their number was wounded by the grenade. They stopped the attack. The villagers did not dare leave the shelters until it was dark, and only then did --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic --

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: -- only then did they form a column and leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: There is something that is unclear to me, and I believe that it is unclear to some other people, too. When the fighting stopped, the HVO soldiers entered the village. Some HVO soldiers did enter the village. You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speakers will have to stop overlapping. It is impossible to interpret.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All the other villagers were in the second half of the village -- in the other half of the village; is that what you're trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the exception of those who lived in the -- on the outskirts of the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Those people were not in the way of the HVO soldiers who had entered the village?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell us, then, that a part of the village of Stupni Do, on the 23rd, was not entered by the HVO soldiers; that the population living in those parts of the village were not touched by anyone; and that as soon as it got dark, those villagers were able to leave the village, to hide in the woods and then managed to save their lives by escaping as it was described? Is that what you're trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I said a little while ago, Abid Likic, when they reached the last destination, there were just two or three house that is were not taken yet, and it is in that house that most of the civilians were. He lobbed two hand grenades on them, they were wounded, and the attack stopped at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us focus on these two or three houses. You told us a little while ago that they were in the part of the village that the HVO did not enter. Now you said two or three houses. Does that mean that the HVO went through the whole of the village and held under control all the houses in Stupni Do, with the exception of those two or three houses, or did I misunderstand you?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: It did not establish control over those two or three houses. This is where those civilians were left. That's what I explained.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. So the HVO controlled all the houses, with the exception of those two or three houses in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And all 170 inhabitants of Stupni Do, let us use that figure, were in those two or three houses?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, more or less, yes, plus/minus ten.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, were all the civilians there right from the beginning of the conflict, or did they move from one shelter to another as the conflict progressed to get further away from the axis of the attack of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were fleeing, they were fleeing, they were saving -- trying to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you talked about the people, the civilians who were killed in the first part of the village, you said that some of them had been disabled. Some are described as very young people, children, really. Can we then conclude that in the first part of the village, only those people were left who were less mobile, so to speak, and who could not move quickly enough to shelters that were further away from the axis of the HVO attack?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, could you please tell us, how come that if you suspected that the HVO might attack Stupni Do, how come that the BH army did not take care of the people who were less mobile, to evacuate them promptly, or at least to move them further away from the axis of the HVO attack?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat this for the third time: The village had been encircled for a year and a half. We had to go through the woods to get the food. The location of this local commune is such that it is surrounded by the Croatian villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, I understand all of that, but the fact is that 170 people were able to save their lives. It is a fact that the people who were less mobile could not be saved. That's what you told us yourself.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So my question is: If there were any indications that there would be an attack, an army first has to think about how to protect its citizens who are disabled or less mobile for other reasons. So can you explain to us why did you fail to take care of those people who were not able to move on time?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I was not aware that there would be an attack. The civilians that managed to get out, I explained to you a little while ago, they fell into the hands of the HVO soldiers again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, these HVO soldiers, did they meet them and did they take them to the UNPROFOR base and were people saved in that way?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I'm -- an UNPROFOR vehicle came by. They would have returned them to Vares. That's what they wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In any case, there is no doubt in your mind that these people were taken care of and saved?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that some of these people were thankful to the HVO for the fact that they had been saved and how they had been saved? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can share with you the example of my mother. My mother --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, I am happy that you're aware of such cases. This brings me to an end of my cross-examination. Mr. Mahmutovic, I would like to thank you.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. You do not allow me to finish my sentences. My mother was recaptured. She was recaptured. They tied a dog to her body, a very dangerous dog, and they were to exchange her for one of their soldiers. That's how they saved people, and for what people had to be thankful to them? She was an elderly woman. She was 60. Before that, she had seen with her own two eyes how they killed her son.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, I'm very sorry that this happened. There is no reason at all for me to doubt your words, but we have not read any such thing in any of the reports, either by the UNPROFOR or the European monitors or any other organisation. We are rather well informed about the destiny of any citizen of Stupni Do who -- whom something bad had happened.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: There is my mother's statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It hasn't been presented to us in this courtroom, and I'm really sorry to hear that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to follow up a bit, because you seem to have given an ironic answer. When counsel asked you whether you were aware of people from Stupni Do being grateful to the HVO, you said yes. But then you gave an example which, of course, illustrates rather the contrary. Now, I'm repeating the question: Are you aware of any people from your village that were, for some reason or other, grateful to the HVO? I'm not aware of the foundation for this question, but there it is. I'm sorry, I have not heard your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me, Your Honours, I would like to tell Judge Trechsel what the foundation for my question is. I believe that after a large number of witnesses and a relatively large number of statements and a relatively large number of the latest statements contained in the UNPROFOR report, we were clear on the fact that the HVO received people who had left Stupni Do, that they transferred them to the UNPROFOR bases, and that was my foundation for the questions that I put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Praljak's Defence has 50 minutes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the opportunity with regard to your defence dated 10 May, and especially paragraph 11 and 12 of this decision. I would like to ask you to allow the Accused Praljak to put the questions to the witness. We have learned a lot of things about Stupni Do so far. It is not in dispute that this was an armed conflict, that this was fighting that took place in the village and around the village. And given the context of the fighting, and given the consequences that to a certain extent are rather dubious, and bearing in mind that Praljak was a soldier, that he was familiar with the situation, that he was clear on the circumstances under which such events happened, I believe that he meets the criteria of the decision because he has specialist knowledge and he is better-suited to put questions on this area. That it would be my oral submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, can you answer a question from the Chamber? General Praljak was not present at the time, was he? Did he have any knowledge about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true, Your Honours, that General Praljak was not there, and we have seen from some of the documents and from the words of certain witnesses that he had been briefed subsequently. We know that there was a certain investigation; in other words, he was subsequently informed about all the details. That's one foundation. The other foundation is that similar events, i.e., conflicts between the army attacking and the army defending irrespective of who the attacker and who the defender was, evolved in a similar ways following similar regularities. In that respect, he has special experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, to be more accurate, what kind of military issue of a technical nature will he talk about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you wish, Your Honours, Mr. Praljak has added some things during the testimony of this witness. He could inform you better than me. I can provide you some general information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have the floor. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much. I have been charged with the events in Stupni Do; although, as you said it yourself, I was not there. I was 200 kilometres away from there, but I was still charged with Stupni Do in the indictment. In addition to being there, there are also statements of the witnesses which form the factual basis, but there is only a logic that puts these facts in a certain relation; for example, the logic about the exact number of trenches around Stupni Do, how far they were apart from each other - I've prepared a little map - the fact whether Bogos is seven kilometres away from Stupni Do, whether these trenches were three or four kilometres away from Stupni Do, further on whether the units of the BiH army in Stupni Do also had machine-guns and how many. This has been omitted. Thank you very much. Cross-examination by Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As you've already heard, I'm going to try and clarify certain matters and certain technical and military matters, as well as some other facts, and I'm going to try and put them in certain perspectives. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to put before us a map on the thing over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On this map, you will see some markings. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Can you put the part with the circles.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You will see eight circles there, marking the village of Kopjari. Can you see that? Witness, can you please look at the map: The village of Kopjari; the village of Dragojevici; Mijakovici; Lijesnica, that's a hill top; Bogos hill; Stupni Do; Mir and Dastansko villages. I'm going to ask you this: During the attack on Stupni Do, did you know that the units of the BiH army of the 3rd Corps had attacked the villages of Kopjari, Dragojevici, and Mijakovici several days before that?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Along the axis indicated by the green arrow pointing towards Vares, were you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I've heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You can see that to Stupni Do and Mir and Bogosi have been marked. You said that a while ago that Stupni Do is some seven kilometres away from Bogos hill. This map that you have is in the scale of 1:100.000, and that means that seven kilometres to be seven centimetres on the map. Would you agree with me that it is not at all possible if you look at the map, and you will see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I'm somewhat lost. The Bogosi hill is seven kilometres away from the village, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if you walk there on foot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On foot. Seven kilometres on foot. Seven kilometres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have to go to Mir, then there are serpentines, you have to negotiate a trail up the meadows; and Mr. Praljak is talking about the distance as the crow flies. As the crow flies, it may be one or two kilometres; but in order for you to climb, you can't go straight. You could if you were a mountain climber, an alpinist. That's the whole point. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. You will agree with me that the houses in Stupni Do are rather scattered and that the distance between the houses on the left side to the right-hand side is about one kilometre and a half, would that be correct, if we consult the map?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Praljak. I did not understand your question at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll take it slowly. Is it correct that the village of Stupni Do is rather elongated, so that one from side of the village to the other side of the village, the distance is about a kilometre and a half at least?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Here I've also marked the lines of the Republika Srpska army in red. Will you agree with me that this is more or less how the things were at the time?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I can't really see this map very well. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Look at the red colour?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can see the red colour, but nothing is legible on the map, so I'm not able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Look at Dastansko towards Zvijezda?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, to better understand where the Bogos hill is and where the village is, we have a photograph which has been given to us by the Prosecution. Could we put it on the ELMO, please, and the witness could then tell us where the Bogos hill stands which would make everything much clearer. We have a photograph here. Can we see the Bogos hill here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on the right-hand side, you can see this rather large hill. Here, on the right-hand side of the map, there is a meadow. You can see that towards the centre, and there is a little forest. And from there, on the right-hand side, Bogos hill starts, but it is not depicted in the picture. That's where it starts. It's a very steep slope, and it goes towards the right side, but it's not depicted in this photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can just see the beginning of it. Right. Please proceed, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I have also marked by an arrow that goes from Vares to Dastansko. This has nothing to do with you. But just for the information of the Trial Chamber, according to your knowledge at that time and later on, was this road that the HVO soldiers and Croats used to withdraw from Vares when the BiH army had attacked Vares, and they went to Dastansko?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Can I have the IC number for this map, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could we have an IC number of the map with circles on it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map shall be given Exhibit number IC 754. Thank you, Your Honour. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Can this piece of paper also be placed on the same place so that we may take a look, merely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: A witness drew this map, and I'm not going to say his name. He is supposed to appear before this Trial Chamber. We have received this map from the Prosecutor's Office, and this map depicts seven trenches, seven trenches around the village from number 1 to number 7. According to your knowledge, is this a true marking of the trenches that were placed around the village of Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Just bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, please, could you explain the meaning of this circle and number 3 next to it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's that trench. This witness claims that there was a trench here, a BiH army trench, or a trench of the forces that were in Stupni Do. He also made a sketch of the roads around the village, and he also drew the seven trenches around the village. Do you agree with this sketch? It's not a map; it's actually a sketch, a drawing. Can you agree with it?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with everything, except for number 3. I don't know what that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. It's enough. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the IC number for this sketch, please, and then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you correct the distances that you provided to the Trial Chamber? You will see -- you will see it on the film. Can you agree that this the distances were not two or three kilometres, that these trenches were much closer to the village?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I never measured any of these distances. I didn't have a tape measure or anything else. But judging by the logic of the thing, if the distance between Vares and Majdan and Stupni Do, if that's two kilometres and 800 metres, it's only logical that all these trenches were between two and seven kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you want to stick to that, be my guest. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Can I please have an IC number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What will be the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit number IC 755. Thank you, Your Honour. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your statement, and I'm reading from the statement that was provided to us by the Prosecutor's Office, you said that you heard the first shots around 8.00 in the morning and that you thought that it was some lads fooling around because that had sometimes happened.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There had been provocations before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then you heard from the surrounding hills not only infantry weapons but also some heavy weaponry, artillery weaponry, and particularly the answer aircraft cannons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The aircraft cannons ranging between 20, 40 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was their target as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And then you say that they targeted the houses at the beginning of the village, in the lower part of the village?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And that that was the inflammatory bullets that set houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that the lines were falling, you were in a trench, then you saw 19 soldiers advancing from the direction of the forest, and then you returned to your house to the shelter there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: But I never entered the shelter. I came to the door of my house, and I told them to that they had to leave, that they had to leave the shelter, all of them to go to the forest, to take the road to the rocky part of the forest in order to save themselves because the line on Bogos, the first line of defence on Bogos, had fallen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you say that half of the people from the shelter who were women and children reached the forest safely. You are saying here that children and women, regardless of the bullets falling around them, had reached the forest safely; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: What I said is correct. I was watching the first group of people that left the shelter. The four of them jumped over the fence. If you understand what I'm saying, they jumped over the fence that was below the house, and they went towards the forest, and they were followed by the others. However, the shooting was so strong that they were afraid to proceed, and they returned to the shelter. They didn't dare proceed. But I didn't know that they had returned to the shelter because I with my father had headed towards the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I understand you, sir, but the fact that they returned because of the shooting is not part of your statement, and I'm glad that you've clarified. You didn't know that they had returned?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And afterwards, you too went closer to the woods where there was an underground shelter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you stayed there until late afternoon or early evening, as we already heard, which was when you went back, and you stated that half of the village was on fire and the other half of the village was not on fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You encountered a neighbour in the fields. His name is ML. I'm not going to give you his full name. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. We have dealt with this. But I'm now interested in the following: You stated that you know that 38 people died or were killed in Stupni Do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, you have to understand that I have to ask this for the simple reason that we are trying to come to the truth about Stupni Do. I'm going to show you a film that was taken by UNPROFOR, by UNPROFOR police that conducted an investigation, after it entered the village of Stupni Do. So my question to you will be the following before we go on to show you the clip: In the meantime, between the arrival of UNPROFOR and the departure of the people from Stupni Do, did anyone bury the people, the dead people, in Stupni Do? Did anyone bury any of the dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The people from Stupni Do, and you yourself, left in the night between the 23rd and the 24th of October 1993. After that, UNPROFOR came in, I think it was on the 25th -- or rather, the 26th. It entered the village of Stupni Do, and some footage was filmed showing everything that could be seen there; and at that moment, 15 or 16 bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My first question to you is the following: In the meantime, did anyone bury any of those people who died or were killed, or was the scene intact until the arrival of UNPROFOR to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to my knowledge, and what I know is true, the HVO in Vares did not allow UNPROFOR to enter the village for three days after the attack, for three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, we know that. This is not controversial.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: None of the villagers could not and did not dare to get in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Why I'm going to ask you to watch closely, and I apologise in advance because I'm sure that this -- that you will be affected by watching this film. It will take you back to everything that you lived through, but I have to show it to you. Why? You told us that sometime on the 4th or the 5th of November, you had gone back to Stupni Do, that you went to the burned out remains of the buildings, and that you took three or four days to dig out all the bodies from the charred debris. So now we will see what the houses looked like, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Praljak, on line 12 of page 86, there is an answer which has a double negative: "None of the villages could not and did not dare to get in there. That means that all the villagers could and dared to get in there." Is that what you wanted to say, witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, Your Honour. Nobody dared to go back there until Vares was liberated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. Excuse me, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This was a double negation. Any way, let us look at P06321.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So is it correct that now we can see the basement, the shelters, the windows, we can see the sandbags around those windows in the background? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I don't know what's going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have seen the terrible images in another film, and the charred bodies of the people who came to be autopsied. I don't know how the autopsy was carried out. We will see them standing around locations where there was no burning, and there had been no burning. His Honour Judge Antonetti noticed that, too, when we first saw this film. What I am bothered about is how the bodies in this other film came to be charred beyond recognition when those houses that we are about to see cannot burn to such a degree. You can see the roofs, the structures, and people inside could have some burns and could perhaps suffocate; but how could some bodies be burnt beyond recognition? Did you -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could you please stop there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you look for an answer to that question? Here, we can see three women who had been killed. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this is very visible or not, or how clear we can get it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The woman, the first woman here, is in a military uniform. My question to you is whether there was a woman among the BH army troops in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, this image could be of better quality. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could we please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You can see she is wearing a camouflage uniform, and below her there are two other women. In the background, we can see those images, we can see the sandbags. We can't see the windows does, though. Another question that I'm going to ask you is whether you know for a fact that from those basements that were protected, that there was no fire on the HVO troops?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So nobody opened fire from the houses?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My next question is: If you were in one position from 8.00 a.m. onwards and then you left this place and you were with your father at one point, so I'm asking you how do you know that? I'm asking you to distinguish between what you really knew was going on in the village that was a kilometre and a half long, and what you learnt subsequently. At that time, on the 23rd, in the morning and during the day, were you in a position to know and to see that fire was not opened from the houses, from the basements, on the HVO, or was that something that you could not know? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could you please stop there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You have to stop the picture here, please. We can -- could we see once again the previous sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stop here. This seems to be a body, calcinated body, and I can notice that all around the body there are no traces of burning. If there had been some combustion, that whole area would have been blackened. Do you know, Witness, why and how is it that aside from that calcinated body, nothing else seemed to be burned around it? I am putting there question to you because there is a hypothesis according to which the calcinated body may have been brought there after wards, after the fact, and that the body may have been burnt elsewhere. What do you say to this hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't recall this building, specifically; and since the image is a bit blurred, if I could see the building from the outside, then I could tell precisely whose building that was, whose house that was, and who was on -- who is depicted here. But as it is now, I cannot tell that. It is not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, you also told us that you were able to identify all the bodies that were found. Could you explain how you could identify a body charred like this one, assuming it is, but that's what we are told.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The easiest way to identify the victims was through the relatives, the survivors, mothers, fathers, grandmothers, grandfathers, because they knew the precise location where the victim was left, either dead or wounded, and this was our main source. This is what helped us most to identify the victims. To be quite specific, at Ejub Likic's house, I was able to retrieve seven burnt bodies: Two small children, his wife, his sister-in-law, his brother, and his mother. He helped me in that. They were all in the basement; and once we dug them out, we were able to ascertain that they had been in the basement. So in most cases, we were assisted by the next of kin to identify the victims. This was done also at the town cemetery in Visoko when efforts were made to identify the victims. We didn't have the DNA analysis, but we had relatives identify them because parts of bodies would be remain whole. They were parts of bodies that were not burned. I remember a little girl whose foot remained intact. The rest of her body was charred. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is yet another body in another house, not the same one. We can see that walls are white and only the ceiling had caved in. It is obviously, I don't know, a child or I can't -- I don't know who did the analysis. But when the Judges asked their questions, it is really difficult for me to accept that these people were burnt right here on these locations. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] But can we move -- can we move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You can see we have a mortar shell. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could we please stop here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is this a mortar shell, a part of a mortar shell, not a 60 millimetre mortar shell but a larger calibre? You can see a barrel or a tube next to it. Are you sure that mortars were not fired from the village?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How can you be sure?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know what we had, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But this was filmed by UNPROFOR, not by Praljak unfortunately. So I'm asking how could UNPROFOR in the village of Stupni Do on the 26th film everything that they saw? They saw 16 bodies, one was doubtful. They saw the houses that had been set on fire, houses that had collapsed, and they also saw this mortar shell. Whence is this mortar shell here?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Let me explain to the Judges, Mr. Praljak. UNPROFOR forces entered the village after the HVO gave its approval, and this footage was made by UNPROFOR. So there are living witnesses who filmed that. Let me put it this way: They picked up the bodies that were visible. They were either whole or charred. They put them into their APCs, and they took them in to the town cemetery in Visoko. So the first 16 persons, these are the persons. So in order to get at the truth, we have to ask them, one of them, the difference. The rest of the people were underneath the rubble. They only took away the bodies that were visible on the surface, and we went after the ones that were under the rubble. So there was this difference in the reports. 16, 38; 16, 38. People kept saying, "Well, 16 people were found, 16 people were found by UNPROFOR."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I would like you to explain for the Chamber this picture. I see on the right something blurred; then a piece of a -- of a tube; then something that could be a mortar grenade, half hidden under what may be paper bags or something; and to the left of that, again something which has more or less the form of a mortar grenade. Do you agree? Do I see it correctly, interpret the picture correctly? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, definitely. This thing to the right, mortar shells are kept in some kind of a casing, just as you would a piece of paper. This thing to the right should be the casing where this mortar shell was supposed to be. That's my explanation based on what I know, and I do know a couple of things. This is how you actually package mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But at any rate, sir, an UNPROFOR witness, a police officer who was in charge of the whole investigation, told us that the investigation had been carried out under their auspices. You told us that in the first month - and this does not tally with what he had said - that the search for the dead bodies lasted until March 1994. I asked him how many new victims were found each month to increase the total for the victims in Stupni Do, and he was unable to explain, to tell me that. Now I'm asking you, with which UNPROFOR members, where, at which houses, were you able to find the remaining bodies, the difference between the 16 and the 38 bodies? So which UNPROFOR member, in which houses did you dig, and when did do you that? So which house had been destroyed to such an extent that the body was buried under the rubble, yet the buildings -- the only ceilings had caved in on those buildings? Now let us look at those houses that had been set on fire by incendiary bullets to what extent that they were actually burnt.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Including your own house. I will show you your own house. You can see, well, there is no roof there, but we can't see the kind of rubble, at least not on these houses, that would necessitate that kind of excavation to get at the victims. You will answer when, where, with whom, from UNPROFOR, you actually did the digging?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the name of that UNPROFOR member. Those were their police officers. They had -- they were armed. They had cameras. And in Milos Rozevic's house, we found a body -- the body, Alija Likic's body. His father name was Osman. Ostoja Danilo's house is destroyed to this day. There is another house where we found Alija, and there was another house that was also destroyed. This is where we found the two disabled persons who had been burnt down. So there are quite a few buildings that haven't yet been renovated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is not controversial, but we have those charred bodies and nothing else. Look at the houses here. They are burned down. They are destroyed, but there was fighting. A crime was committed. This is not in dispute here, but the extent of this crime is something that I am really fixated on. When were you able to dig out the remaining people to make up the difference between the 16 and the 38 victims? The investigation ended in March, yet the number of victims kept growing. Was the investigation really completed in March, or did new victims of Stupni Do emerge later?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the exact date when I completed the investigation. I explained to the Trial Chamber that only one victim out of the 38 has not yet been found, and I learned later from a witness what happened to that person. But as for all the others, I don't remember whether it lasted a month or a month and a half; but at any rate, I was able to find and bury all the victims. I explained about all those cases. If I am not speaking the truth, there are other victims -- witnesses. There is footage taken by the Nordic Battalion, and they filmed and they were present when I found Likic, Alija. That's just one example.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We had a man here who showed us some really ugly photographs here of the 16 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You just mentioned something, sir. When you found the bodies, you say that the Nordic Battalion was already there. Did they take any pictures? Did they the shoot a video as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Apart from the 16 bodies - one was doubtful here, too - we did not see any photographs taken in the course of the excavation, exhumation, or the bodies themselves, because the bodies would be completely decomposed after a month and a half, and given that there had been raining -- there had been rain. We never saw any photographs of those bodies being exhumed or taken anywhere. We have the information only regarding the 16. So I'm just asking whether anyone would bring here photographs that would show what really happened in Stupni Do, but let us not dwell on is that. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] You can take all of this away.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you some more questions. Sir, a witness says that there were 43 guards in the village, and he says that since there were seven guard posts, there were three men on each of them, 21 men per shift. We had people say there were 20 people, and this guy says 43. And you were not a commander, but is it possible that in Stupni Do there were 43 armed people, as a protected witness testified?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Praljak. The shifts were -- these were not real soldiers. The shifts were like the shifts that you would have in a factory. People did not take their weapons home. A soldier would go to do his shift; and after 12 hours, he would hand over the rifle to another soldier to replace him, and he would go home.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. So this witness says there were 43 of them, and he goes on to say that the worst guard post was Potok, the stream, because it was located between two hills and it was the place that was very good for an attack. So anyone guarding that post would be in dire straits if they had to defend against an attack there. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: This was a post halfway between the village of Stupni Do and Vares Majdan. Now, as to whether it was really that dangerous or not, I'm not a military analyst. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is it true, according to you, that on that day, there were five people -- at least five people at Bogos from your village?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figure. I know that two people were killed in the trench. They remained there. I know that Ejub Likic was there, and I know that he ran out of the trench leaving his rifle behind. He ran to the village. He's mentioned here. I know that the father of one of the lads who got killed up there went in that direction. He was unarmed, and he was shot and killed by the HVO halfway up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So Momir and his father, Salkin Sekjia [phoen], were all killed?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And then he says that they prepared for the fight and the fighting that ensued lasted two and a half hours. Are you familiar with the fact that on one of these positions - and apparently this is the position which is close to Bogos - that the fighting lasted for two hours and a half and that the distance between the attackers and the defence was 50 metres?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that apart from this group that was in the centre of the village, as this one witness put it, not in the shelters of two or three houses, do you know that a group of about 40 people had pulled out earlier, going through the woods to the HVO check-point, where they were given water, UNPROFOR was called, and they were transferred to the free territory, territory controlled by the BH army? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Praljak, but I think that this is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine, fine. I'm just talking about testimony that we heard.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know about that, and I can't tell you things that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. You just tell us what you know, and we will be able to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Before we do, Your Honours, if I may. I will need about four minutes for redirect, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] No problems. I will conclude briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me just tell you this: Are you aware of the fact that a statement -- that a witness said that: "Near our trench at Stensiska [phoen], I saw the dead body of Zejnil Mahmutovic. He had a very large wound on his back caused by a dumdum bullet." Do you know that Zejnil Mahmutovic was killed next to the trench?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: This was my father, and I know for a fact where he was killed. I know that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. I didn't know that. I didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just explain. There was no trench there. This was a place above those houses. The last time that I left my father there, he didn't want to leave the two people, the people who couldn't move, who had been -- who later got burnt in the rubble. He didn't want to leave them behind he was such a good man. I found him, or rather, UNPROFOR found him and UNPROFOR took him away. I was able to see him just before the funeral. He had four through-and-through gunshot wounds on his chest, So he was not killed by a dumdum bullet. It was a sower of death, a machine-gun, and the bullet wounds were from the top going to the side. This I can tell because I was able to see him in the coffin.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I just put to you the testimony of a witness who testified as a protected witness. So this is not what I'm claiming. I'm just trying to put together this jigsaw puzzle.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm here just to tell the truth, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Whatever happened - and the Trial Chamber will be able to ascertain that on the basis of various elements in the end, I'm sure - I want to know the following: You claim that at least 500 HVO soldiers, and two of the units as we came to learn, were special units, Maturice and Apostoli, and that they attacked the village that was defended by a certain number of people who had rifles, machine-guns, and whatever. 170 people were gathered in a place. You said that some of those who attacked the village were under the influence of drugs. So how is it possible that if the overall plan was to kill the inhabitants of Stupni Do, how is it possible that an armed force of this magnitude, that included two good units in military terms, that they decided not to attack 170 people defended by a handful of people after just two hand grenades were thrown? Is this possible? If somebody is really bent on killing these people, as you're saying, who would decide not to proceed after only two hand grenades were thrown? Is this, according to you, logical in military terms? We all went through this war, so did you see that or did you just hear stories about that?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: The information about the accurate number of participants in Stupni Do village I read in the autobiography by Mr. Miroslav Pejcinovic -- actually, it was Ante Pejcinovic, the then chief of the Vares HVO, who published a book. The Defence line was very long, and a lot of people were needed to man that line. According to Mr. Pejcinovic, between 400 and 500 men participated, and I'm talking about real soldiers, those who had already participated in fighting. There were about 120 according to his statement, and they were Maturice and Apostoli. The other HVO troops were from our own mess, from the neighbouring villages close to the Stupni Do commune. There was the Pukovnija Brigade from Mir, there was one from Bijelo Polje, from the village of Perizici [phoen], all of which were close to the local commune of Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Just tell me whether you saw anybody throwing hand grenades and whether you saw those soldiers under the influence of drugs giving up on their attempt. Did you see it?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that from the people who were in that atomic shelter that I spoke about a little while ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was that just one atomic shelter or were there more houses? There is no single house in Stupni Do that accommodate 200 people.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: The attack reached the two or three houses that remained there in the bottom part of the village. As for the exact number there were in the first or second or third house, I really can't tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Mahmutovic, if the lines are long and if people withdrew together with the army to the three houses, there are no longer the lines of defence of the BiH army. The HVO was around those three houses. How can there be lines? How could the village had fallen? How come people were in the houses? There is no logic to that.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: You said it, Mr. Praljak, that our soldiers went to the HVO road, that the UNPROFOR took them away.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I was saying -- I was just relating the witness's words. If there were three houses left with a few soldiers that were defending them, that means that the rest had been already captured by the HVO and that the HVO with 150 or 200 troops was around those three houses. And even after the two hand grenades were thrown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have a question which perhaps will clarify matters for the Bench. We had a witness, I will not give his name, who clearly indicated what the purpose of this military operation was. According to him, it was to take control of the Bogos hill. According to this witness, this was a hill of a strategic -- of strategic importance, and enabled the people taking it to control the village. So there was an attack and fighting on this hill, and there were wounded people on the HVO side. Two people were injured. After the attack, the hill was taken and the HVO troops who were not -- there were not 500 soldiers but much less. This is what this witness said to us. Does that fit in with what you saw, Because were you there at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the witness said in that statement that one trench, where there were five BH army soldiers and which was above the village to the left, towards the village of Mir, was never captured. It was never taken. They sent the woman to the trench, the one that the lady lawyer spoke about. They sent the woman with the message for these soldiers to surrender. There were some 20 to 30 soldiers around it, and they were trying the whole day to take it but they never succeeded. That trench was between Mir and Stupni Do. That was the second elevation in terms of strategic significance, and some of those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this trench wasn't taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never. It was never taken, and it was three kilometres away from the village itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the HVO had sent this woman so that these people would surrender? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I adhere to my question. If the lines except for the trench that was never taken, if all the other lines in Stupni Do were taken, and majority of the population, 107 plus/minus were in the three houses, the HVO is all around, then according to your information, the HVO has anti-aircraft cannon that can pierce every wall of those three houses. According to military logic, would take be of these houses have been any problem at all for the HVO force that was there at the time, in your view?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: The moment when the HVO soldiers entered the village, or at least one part of the village, the mortar fire stopped, the mortar fire stopped. The artillery fire because, of course, they would not shoot at their own men. Everything else that happened was by death sowers and the automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. So mortars are easily movable, so are the anti-aircraft cannons, but I won't dwell on that. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Can we please look at P03877.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: There is a photo of your house. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] P083877 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please confirm that this is your house? The roof had burned down. It is not habitable, but it is not devastated. And if you want to dig, there is nothing to dig because what had fallen off from the roof, what had burned down, does not pose a problem and cannot bury anybody who would be underneath.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The house existed, it's still there, it has not been reconstructed. You can see it any day, any time of day. There is also the atomic shelter. Everything is there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, was this: Is it true that there is nothing to dig out from here? If there was anybody dead in the basement, anybody who came up to the house could have seen that person?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the house was absolutely brand new at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not in dispute of that. I'm asking you: The way we see the photo, when the house burned down, when the roof caved in --

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: This is not my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is not your house?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Then this is the problem on the side of the Prosecutor, because the Prosecutor claims that this is your house.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No. A while ago that was my house, in the photo. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Can you please show it again, P08377.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my house. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We don't have that photo. I cannot tell whether this is correct or not. There is no telling. Is this your house?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please, I know it was new. I know that it was torched. All that is correct. But my question is this: If somebody had been killed or died in the shelter outside the shelter around the house, should there have been any digging for these bodies? If there had been a body, you could see it. You didn't have to excavate for it, especially if they were in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, 50 per cent of the houses were old. They were made of wood and bricks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking about your house. You said that something had happened here and that you had to dig for days.

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Not here. Here the people were killed in front of the house. That's why I never attempted to reconstruct it and renovate it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The house -- the Judges can see this on the film. I can't embark on any further analysis. This would be -- thank you very much, sir. I'm sorry I had to show you things that evoke unpleasant memories. I would like to thank the Judges and you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I have to further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, after my learned friend from the Prosecution, I would like to reserve a few minutes that I need. We would have a housekeeping matter, very short, if I can reserve that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we shall, first of all, finish with the witness. The Prosecution, Mr. Flynn? Mr. Flynn, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I limit it to one question, if not two, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, some doubt has been cast on the number of deaths attributable to the attack on Stupni Do and whether all these bodies were bodies that were fallen, people who had fell during the attack on Stupni Do. If you look at the list that you prepared under 8461, the 38 people --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: No, 8461. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Are you in a position to assist the Tribunal in any way to verify this list, other than through information you received from families? For example, how many of these people on this list did you yourself, if you can remember, did you yourself see on the 23rd of October or on the 22nd of October? Did you have occasion to see any of them apart from say your family members? Did you have occasion to meet any of them prior to the attack?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: You mean before they were killed, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question. On this list, I see in your language, the word "borac." I believe this means "soldier." So ten of these people were soldiers, ten.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I saw a majority of these people. I didn't see the children on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And following the attack, did you have occasion to meet any of them immediately after the attack? Did you ever meet any of them again?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, sir. I saw them dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you know if any of them died through natural causes or some other means other than the attack on Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HUSNIJA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Only the elderly woman, Rasema, who died from fear as she was leaving the village. Her name is Rasema Likic. Her father's name is Besmir [phoen]. They left her there to lie on the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must put a very important question to you. This is most important for the Bench. These ten soldiers who are on the list, did they die in combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in combat. Medina [phoen] Likic, she did not die in combat, the one that Mr. Praljak asked me about. She worked as a cook in the BiH army, and she was killed in a trench. We saw the footage when Mr. Praljak asked me about a uniformed woman, that was the woman who was a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the other soldiers? Where did they die during combat operations [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I leave it at that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We do not have your answer, witness, to the question of the President, Where did they die during combat operations? Can you give an answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to go back to the list, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] If you will allow me, Your Honours, the answer to the Honourable Judge's Antonetti's question was not recorded. The question was whether the rest were soldiers and the witness said, "Yes, they were."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'll put the question again, witness. On the list, there are the names of ten soldiers, and my question was a very precise question. As far as you know, those people here who are on the list and who were there on the list as soldiers, did they die in combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, except for my brother who was killed in front of our own house, Edin Mahmutovic, son of Zenil [phoen], and Edina Likic, daughter of Sulejman, who was working as a cook for the army, and she was killed in Kemal Likic's house that we saw. The rest were all killed in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
